name: Common Cobra
description: The Indian cobra (Naja naja) is one of the most dangerous snakes in Asia. Responsible for thousands of snakebite deaths annually in India. Identifiable by its iconic hood when threatened.
symptoms: Ptosis, paralysis, respiratory failure, local pain and swelling
habitat: Agricultural areas, forests, near human settlements

name: Russell's Viper
description: Responsible for the most snakebite deaths in India and Southeast Asia. Its venom causes severe coagulopathy and organ damage. It is aggressive and strikes without much provocation.
symptoms: Severe pain, swelling, bleeding disorders, kidney failure

name: Green Pit Viper
description: Arboreal pit viper with excellent camouflage among green foliage. Bites are painful and cause significant tissue damage, but are rarely fatal with prompt treatment.
symptoms: Severe local pain, swelling, blistering, tissue necrosis
habitat: Trees, shrubs in forests and gardens

name: Common Krait
description: Nocturnal snake with highly potent neurotoxic venom. Bites are often painless and occur during sleep, making them particularly dangerous as they may go unnoticed until symptoms begin.
symptoms: Abdominal pain, ptosis, paralysis, respiratory failure
habitat: Agricultural fields, termite mounds, human dwellings

name: Saw-scaled Viper
description: Small but highly aggressive viper responsible for more human deaths than any other snake in many dry regions. Makes a distinctive rasping sound by rubbing its scales together.
habitat: Arid regions, rocky areas, dry grasslands

name: King Cobra
description: The world's longest venomous snake, reaching up to 5.5 metres. It can deliver a massive amount of venom in a single bite—enough to kill an elephant. Despite its fearsome reputation, it generally avoids humans.
symptoms: Severe pain, dizziness, paralysis, cardiac arrest

name: Black Mamba
description: Africa's most feared snake, known for its speed, aggression when threatened, and highly potent venom. Without antivenom, a bite is nearly always fatal. Named for the black interior of its mouth, not its skin colour.
symptoms: Rapid onset paralysis, respiratory failure, cardiac arrest

name: Copperhead
description: Pit viper with relatively mild venom and responsible for the most snakebites in the eastern United States. Bites are rarely fatal. Named for its copper-coloured head.

name: Green Vine Snake
description: A slender rear-fanged snake perfectly camouflaged among vines and leaves. Its venom is mild and harmless to humans, typically causing only minor local irritation. Not medically significant.

name: Boa Constrictor
description: A large, non-venomous snake that kills prey by constriction rather than venom. Popular in the exotic pet trade. While a bite from a large adult can cause puncture wounds, it poses no toxicological threat.
symptoms: Bite wounds from teeth, possible secondary infection

name: Taipan
description: The coastal taipan is one of Australia's most dangerous snakes. It has the longest fangs of any Australian snake and delivers a large amount of highly potent venom. Related to the inland taipan, the most venomous land snake by LD50.
symptoms: Rapid paralysis, blood clotting disorders, kidney failure
habitat: Sugarcane fields, woodland edges, coastal scrub

name: Puff Adder
description: The puff adder causes more snakebite deaths in Africa than any other species due to its wide distribution and cryptic colouration. It inflates its body and hisses loudly when threatened—the origin of its name.
symptoms: Massive local swelling, necrosis, bleeding, hypotension

name: Eastern Diamondback Rattlesnake
description: The largest rattlesnake species and heaviest venomous snake in the Americas. Its unmistakable rattle serves as a warning. Delivers large quantities of venom per bite.
symptoms: Severe pain, rapid swelling, tissue necrosis, coagulopathy
habitat: Longleaf pine savannas, coastal scrub, palmetto flatwoods

name: Boomslang
description: A rear-fanged arboreal snake whose venom causes a deadly coagulopathy. Bites are rare as it is timid and rear-fanged, but when envenomation occurs it can be lethal within 24 hours without antivenom.
symptoms: Delayed bleeding from multiple sites, organ failure

name: Death Adder
description: Despite its name, the death adder is not a true adder. It has the fastest strike of any Australian snake and injects a highly potent neurotoxin. It relies on camouflage rather than flight, making accidental treading a risk.
